title: The Arithmetic of Survival

narrative.text: Elara Vostane requested this meeting in writing. Not through Vyktor, not through the scheduling office — directly, in a two-paragraph letter on Finance Ministry letterhead that arrived on your desk at eight o'clock on a Tuesday morning. The formality of it told you everything. Elara uses formality the way some people use silence: not as absence but as weight.

Gregor Marić was not on the original invitation list. He found out about the meeting through the cabinet notification system and informed Vyktor that he would be attending. No one told him he couldn't. This is either an oversight or something Elara anticipated and chose not to prevent. With Elara, oversight and intention are difficult to separate.

The projection on the wall behind her chair shows the revised budget position. You do not need to read the numbers carefully to understand that the red column is taller than the one from seventeen weeks ago.

Current annual deficit: ninety-one million Krone, up from sixty-five at the start of the year. Contributors: refugee emergency spending — twelve million. Constitutional convention administrative costs — four million. Revenue shortfall from lower-than-projected Q3 growth — eleven million. And three discretionary decisions made earlier this year that I do not need to characterize because you were in the room when they were made.

At this trajectory, the national debt reaches four hundred and twenty million by the end of fiscal year. That is nineteen point nine percent of GDP, which crosses the threshold the IMA uses to trigger a mandatory credit review. If the IMA conducts a credit review, they will publish their findings. If they publish their findings, Arcturian and Lytheirian institutional investors will reprice Veltrian bonds. The Krone has already declined four point three percent against the Arcturian dollar since September. A credit review accelerates that. Once the Krone falls past a critical point, the debt service burden expressed in real terms increases even if we do not borrow another Krone. I want you to understand what that sentence means.

It means the debt becomes self-generating. It means you can do everything right from this point forward and still lose because of what was done wrong before. It is the fiscal equivalent of a building whose load-bearing walls have been quietly compromised — it stands until it doesn't.

I have modeled a path that stabilizes this. It requires a spending reduction of forty-two million over the next fiscal year. Twenty million from welfare and social programs, fourteen million from infrastructure deferral, eight million from education. In exchange, the deficit trajectory reverses, we avoid the credit review, and by mid-year-two we have sufficient reserve to manage the debt without external intervention. This path works. I have checked it four times.

I am here to tell you that if you choose a different path — if you reject this stabilization package in favour of revenue measures that will take eighteen months to materialise, or foreign borrowing that creates new obligations, or any version of 'let's wait and see' — I will submit my resignation. Not because I am threatening you. Because I cannot in conscience continue to sign documents representing a fiscal position I believe will end in a currency crisis inside eighteen months, and because my name on those documents is a form of endorsement I am not willing to give.
The room holds the silence she intended it to hold. Gregor Marić, who has been listening with the specific quality of attention that means he is preparing to be furious, breathes in through his nose.

I want to tell you what twenty million Krone means in Kravenstal. It means the difference between the winter welfare supplement existing and not existing. It means three social health clinics that serve populations with no other access to medical care. It means the children's nutrition program that we reinstated in the first month of this government because children in this republic were going to school hungry — were going to school hungry, Chancellor, in the wealthiest province by industrial output in this nation — because the Halvek government had decided that a fed child was a less obedient child.

I am not an economist. Elara is correct that I am not an economist. I understand what she is saying about the debt trajectory. I understand that the numbers are real and that the consequences of ignoring them are real. But the people who will absorb twenty million Krone in social program cuts are also real, and they are not abstract risks in a projection model — they are workers who voted for this government because we told them we would not do what every government before us did, which was balance the budget on the back of people who cannot afford to absorb the balancing.

If you implement this austerity package, you will have riots in Kravenstal inside six weeks. I am not predicting it as a political threat. I am telling you what will happen because I know those workers, I have worked alongside them, and I have watched what happens when a government they trusted takes away the only thing standing between their family and the winter. They don't write letters. They go to the streets. And once they're in the streets, the Iron Covenant asks for emergency powers to clear them, and you lose two years of everything we've built in a single month.

I should mention. The IMA has sent a preliminary inquiry. Not official contact yet. Just a letter asking whether we'd be interested in discussing 'financial stability frameworks.' It arrived yesterday. I didn't tell you until now because you had enough on your desk.

They are both right. That is the problem. Elara is right about the numbers and Gregor is right about the people and those two correct things are pointing in opposite directions and you have to choose which correct thing you can live with destroying.

monologue: Elara sent the letter directly. Not through Vyktor — directly, on Finance Ministry letterhead, by eight in the morning. The formality is the message. Forty-two million in cuts. Twenty million from welfare. She has checked the model four times. She is offering competent fiscal management and the destruction of the social compact my government was elected to defend. Gregor says riots in six weeks. Both of them are right. Both of them want me to choose.

choices.text: "The stabilization package. Forty-two million in cuts, the timeline Elara has outlined. I'm not going to tell Kravenstal this is painless — I'll go there myself and explain why we're doing it and what the alternative was. But I will not govern from the edge of a currency crisis."

reactions.text: She nods once — the nod she uses to close a meeting. Then she is already annotating the implementation timeline. She does not thank you. Vostane does not thank people for making the correct fiscal decision. She simply proceeds to execute it.

Marić says nothing. His hands, which had been flat on the table all meeting, are now fists. He does not look at you. He looks at the wall behind your head, at the projection of the budget numbers, at the column showing twenty million from welfare programs. Then he stands and leaves. He does not ask permission. The door swings shut behind him, and the swinging is worse than a slam would have been.

He waits until the door settles. I have drafted a statement for the press. 'The government has implemented a fiscal stabilization package. The package includes targeted spending reductions necessary to maintain national creditworthiness.' He pauses. I have not included the words 'Kravenstal' or 'welfare' anywhere in the statement. That was intentional.

choices.text: "Revenue first, not cuts. A temporary corporate surcharge, an accelerated wealth-tier collection, and a review of BNI and military discretionary spending. We find the money at the top before we take it from the bottom. Elara, I need you to make this work."

reactions.text: He releases the breath he has been holding all meeting. His hands unclench. He does not smile — Marić does not smile at policy victories, he simply stops being tense. It is the closest thing to gratitude you have ever received from him.

Vostane closes her portfolio with exaggerated precision — the precision of someone who is working very hard not to say what she is thinking. She has already calculated the revenue trajectory. The calculation is not encouraging. She does not share it yet. She is too professional to say I told you so before it becomes true.

He writes revenue measures on his notepad and draws a line underneath it. Under the line: Vael capital flight. Expected within four weeks. He does not say it out loud. He simply shows you the page. The warning is more effective for being written rather than spoken.

choices.text: "Respond positively to the IMA inquiry. We negotiate the terms — we don't accept the standard structural adjustment package, but we explore what a tailored facility looks like. The bridge loan buys us the time we need. Elara, please stay."

reactions.text: Vostane is already reaching for the IMA contact file. She does not celebrate — Vostane never celebrates. But something in her posture shifts, the way a bridge engineer's posture shifts when the load calculations finally balance. She has found a path. It is not the path she wanted. But it is a path.

IMA negotiations. He says the words as though tasting something bitter. I understand the logic. I do not like the logic. He pauses. Tell me honestly: is this a loan we negotiate on our terms, or a loan we accept on theirs because the alternative is worse? Because the people in Kravenstal will know the difference, even if the IMA's accountants do not.

choices.text: "I'm not accepting the austerity package, and if that means you resign, Elara, then I am sorry to lose you. Gregor is right about what those cuts mean for real people. I'll find someone who will find a different way through the numbers."

reactions.text: Vostane closes her portfolio with the particular care of someone who has just been told that her professional judgment is not sufficient. She does not argue. She does not respond. She simply stands, removes her glasses, and walks toward the door. The silence is the sound of Elara Vostane accepting that she has lost — not the argument, which she still believes she won, but the decision, which she cannot now unmake.

Marić waits until she is gone. Then he turns to you. His voice is very quiet — the quiet of a man who has just watched someone he respected be dismissed for being right. He says nothing for a long moment. Then he nods. Once. It is not gratitude. It is acknowledgment. The acknowledgment of someone who understands what you just paid to keep the welfare supplement in Kravenstal.

He speaks only after the door closes. Vostane's resignation will be effective immediately. I will brief Halvar. He pauses. You just traded the best finance minister in forty years for six weeks of political capital. I am not judging the trade. I am making sure you have counted it.
